title: As we forgive
hookLine: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors (Matthew 6:12)

lines: A LINE THAT GOES BY FAST.
cards: A stadium before a game. A hospital chapel at night. A classroom, a wedding, a funeral.
Somewhere right now, people are saying the Lord's Prayer together, some fast and some slow, a few half a beat behind. And in the middle comes a line people say so smoothly they sail right past it.
Forgive us, as we forgive. Two words sit in that line like a hinge: as we. The person praying asks for mercy, and in the same breath ties that mercy to their own.

teach.h: DEBTS: A WRONG AS A BILL.
teach.b: Start with the words Jesus taught, in Matthew's Gospel. The King James has it: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Debts.
The picture is a ledger: somebody owes, and forgiving means letting the bill go unpaid. Second, the other versions.
Luke's Gospel gives the prayer a little differently: "forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us."
And the Book of Common Prayer, the Church of England's prayer book, says trespasses: "forgive us our trespasses, As we forgive them that trespass against us."
Debts, sins, trespasses. Churches still say it different ways, and each word lights a different corner of the same room. Third, the hinge.

teach.h: THE ONE LINE THE TEXT UNDERLINES.
teach.b: Right after the prayer, Matthew has Jesus come back to one line: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."

teach.h: A MIRROR: WHAT DO I HOLD?
teach.b: Of all the prayer's lines, this is the one the text stops to underline. Christians read it more than one way. Some hear a condition: mercy received and mercy given come as a pair.

Others hear a description: a heart that has really taken in forgiveness starts to give it away, the way a full cup spills. Christian teachers have argued over that balance, and the prayer holds it without settling it.
Fourth, the plain fact of saying it.

Each time someone prays this line, they name their own debts and their debtors in one sentence. For anyone, praying or not, that's a mirror: what am I asking to be let off, and what am I still holding over someone else?

how: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer in private and together in church; depending on the church and the translation, the line says debts, sins or trespasses.

o: wrongs done against you, as one prayer book words it
walking onto land without the owner's permission
small rules broken by accident, not on purpose

games.q: one prayer, three words — tap the pairs.
p: if ye forgive men their trespasses

s: every version of the Lord's Prayer says trespasses
Matthew in the King James says debts; Luke says sins; the Book of Common Prayer says trespasses.
right after the prayer, Matthew comes back to the forgiveness line
"for if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."
Christians all read 'as we forgive' the same way

games.q: Jesus has just finished teaching the prayer. of all its lines, which one does Matthew have him come straight back to?
o: give us this day our daily bread.
games.why: the forgiveness line: "for if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." it's the one the text stops to underline.

practice: Bring to mind one modest debt someone owes you, a borrowed book, an apology that never came, a favor not returned, and see their name on one line of a ledger.
Picture tearing up that line, not because it didn't matter, but because you choose to stop collecting, and notice what happens in your chest.
If you pray, you can say the line from the Lord's Prayer slowly, with that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Trespasses. One Christian version's word for the wrongs forgiven in the Lord's Prayer, debts in Matthew, sins in Luke. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from Matthew 6:12: debts, what is owed.
